visualLead: A line guides the eye. Direction, weight and movement can make it hurry, wander or stop.
textLead: A sentence guides a reader through an idea. Length and structure control pace and direction.
visualVocab: Direct and controlled; the eye travels without a detour.
Soft and changing; the eye follows a gentle turn.
Sharp changes create energy, tension or surprise.
textVocab: One complete idea moves in a clear direction.
Two complete ideas travel side by side.
A main idea changes direction through a dependent clause.
Although it rained, we continued.
lab: The road curved past the market and into the fading light.
Both carry the eye forward gently.

visualLead: Color changes mood before we name what an image shows. Temperature and saturation carry feeling.
textLead: Diction means word choice. Connotation gives language its emotional color.
visualVocab: Reds, oranges and yellows often feel energetic or welcoming.
Blues and blue-greens often feel calm, distant or controlled.
Low saturation feels restrained, soft or serious.
textVocab: Glowing, welcome and lively create emotional warmth.
Crisp, still and distant create emotional coolness.
lab: The room glowed with lively conversation.
Warm color and warm words feel close and active.
The room held a crisp, distant silence.
Cool color and cool words create distance.
The room settled into subdued conversation.
Less saturation and quieter diction lower intensity.

visualLead: Shapes create boundaries and recognizable structures. Their silhouette helps us predict how to read them.
textLead: Whole texts also have shapes: information can narrow, widen, leave and return.
visualVocab: A wide base and narrow point create direction and stability.
Wide ends meet at a narrow turning point.
A continuous edge returns to where it began.
textVocab: News begins with the most important facts, then narrows into detail.
A story builds toward a turning point, then resolves.
The ending returns to an image or idea from the opening.
lab: Who, what, where first; details follow.
The text narrows from essential facts to supporting detail.
A student misses a bus, adapts, and arrives changed.
The middle turning point gives the hourglass its waist.
It opens at the river and returns there at the end.
The ending closes the same loop the opening began.

visualLead: Texture makes a surface feel rough, smooth, heavy or light—even when we only see it.
textLead: Sound and rhythm give language texture. Consonants can scrape; vowels can flow.
visualVocab: Irregular marks make a surface feel coarse or resistant.
Even surfaces and gentle transitions feel calm and easy.
Small repeated marks add visible material.
textVocab: Repeated opening sounds create a noticeable verbal surface.
K, t and cr sounds can feel clipped or rough.
Long vowels and connected phrases feel smooth.
lab: Hard consonants behave like a rough surface.
Long sounds and even rhythm reduce friction.
Tiny repeated sounds add fine texture.

visualLead: Form adds depth. Light, shadow and viewpoint reveal that an object has more than a surface.
textLead: Subtext is meaning below the literal words. Context reveals what a speaker does not say directly.
visualVocab: Shading makes a flat shape feel solid.
Highlights show which surface faces the source.
A shadow suggests depth beyond the visible edge.
textVocab: The exact surface meaning of the words.
A meaning suggested by context, not directly stated.
The attitude that shapes how the words are understood.
lab: Without context, only the surface is visible.
“Nice work,” she said, looking at the broken chair.
Context adds a second meaning: criticism.
The unsaid concern casts a shadow beneath polite words.

visualLead: Space gives elements room, separates groups and lets the eye rest.
textLead: Silence appears as pauses, paragraph breaks and deliberate omission. It gives meaning room.
visualVocab: The area occupied by the main subject.
The open area around and between subjects.
A quiet boundary protects content from the edge.
textVocab: Punctuation creates a small silence inside a sentence.
A larger silence marks a turn in idea, time or speaker.
Leaving something unsaid can invite inference.
lab: We arrived we sat we spoke we left.
No open space or pauses make both forms hard to enter.
We arrived. We sat. Then we spoke.
Small gaps and sentence stops create usable rhythm.
A large gap makes silence meaningful.

visualLead: Typefaces have posture and personality. Size, weight and spacing influence how words sound in the mind.
textLead: Emphasis and voice reveal who seems to speak—and which words deserve attention.
visualVocab: Small finishing strokes often feel established or formal.
Soft corners often feel friendly or playful.
textVocab: Language can be formal, neutral or casual for different situations.
Emphasizing one word changes the sentence's focus.
Patterns of word choice and rhythm create a recognizable speaker.
lab: Please submit the document by noon.
A formal serif posture fits an official register.
Rounded forms fit an inviting voice.
Heavy weight and short wording intensify emphasis.

visualLead: Contrast makes difference visible: light against dark, large beside small, still beside active.
textLead: Antithesis places opposing ideas in parallel form so their difference becomes clear.
visualVocab: A large form beside a small one creates emphasis.
Similar forms feel quiet and less distinct.
textVocab: Opposing ideas appear in balanced grammatical form.
Many are called; few are chosen.
Two unlike images or ideas sit beside each other.
Matching grammar makes the opposition easier to see.
To err is human; to forgive, divine.
lab: Strong opposites in matching forms create a sharp edge.
One voice whispered; a thousand answered.
Large numerical difference creates scale contrast.
The room was calm and quiet.
Related words create harmony rather than opposition.

visualLead: Hierarchy tells the eye what to notice first, second and third.
textLead: Information architecture orders ideas so readers can find the point, key detail and background.
visualVocab: The strongest element attracts attention first.
A supporting element attracts attention next.
textVocab: Gives the most important supporting information.
Adds context after the reader knows the point.
The building closed in June following flood damage.
lab: Visible levels give the reader a reliable path.
The reader must decide what matters without help.
Hiding the point creates delay or confusion.

visualLead: Alignment creates invisible lines that make separate elements feel organized.
textLead: Parallelism aligns grammar. Items in a series feel connected when they share the same form.
visualVocab: Elements share a left, right, top or bottom edge.
One element breaks the shared line and attracts attention.
textVocab: List items use the same verb form.
We came; we saw; we learned.
One item changes form and feels crooked.
lab: to read, to write, to speak
Shared visual edges match shared grammatical forms.
One changed form breaks the pattern.
The correction restores both rhythm and expectation.

visualLead: Balance distributes visual weight. Symmetry feels stable; asymmetry feels dynamic.
textLead: Punctuation distributes the weight of clauses. It separates, balances or interrupts ideas.
visualVocab: Equal forms on either side feel formal and steady.
Unequal forms find equilibrium through contrast.
Forms balance around a central point.
textVocab: Balances two complete, closely related clauses.
Interrupts the line and throws emphasis to one side.
Separates ideas into independent units with a clean stop.
lab: The room grew quiet; the speaker began.
The semicolon holds equal complete clauses in balance.
The plan looked simple—but one detail changed everything.
The em dash makes a dramatic asymmetrical shift.
The room grew quiet. The speaker began.
The period gives each idea its own stable space.

visualLead: Items placed near each other appear related. Distance marks where one group ends and another begins.
textLead: Related sentences share a paragraph. A break creates meaningful distance between ideas.
visualVocab: Small distance says: these belong together.
Large distance says: these are separate groups.
Consistent spacing makes several items one unit.
textVocab: Gathers sentences that develop one controlling idea.
Signals a new idea, time, speaker or focus.
Repeated key words and links hold nearby ideas together.
lab: Rain filled the street. Buses moved slowly.
Close forms and related sentences read as one group.
Inside, the meeting began on time.
Distance and a paragraph break mark a new focus.
Street details together; meeting details together.
Two clusters make two relationships visible.

visualLead: Repetition builds pattern, unity and recognition by bringing a form back.
textLead: Anaphora repeats an opening; inclusio repeats at the end to create a verbal bookend.
visualVocab: A recognizable form returns across a design.
A repeated form changes once to create interest.
textVocab: Successive lines begin with the same words.
We will learn. We will build.
The ending repeats the opening to frame the whole text.
lab: We will listen. We will learn. We will lead.
Repeated openings create rhythm and unity.
The river welcomed us … We returned to the river.
We came to learn, to test, to change—and to learn again.
One change prevents repetition from becoming flat.

visualLead: Simplicity removes anything that does not help the message. Fewer elements give important ones more force.
textLead: Concision removes words that do not add meaning. The idea becomes easier to see.
visualVocab: Every remaining element has a job.
Competing elements make the main point hard to find.
textVocab: Two expressions repeat the same meaning.
Words occupy space without advancing the idea.
It is important to note that…
The shortest clear form keeps the full meaning.
lab: At this point in time, we are currently ready.
Extra objects and repeated words hide the point.

visualLead: A design succeeds when its form helps it do its job. A map, poster and warning need different choices.
textLead: Genre is a form shaped by purpose. A CV, story and essay arrange language differently because they do different jobs.
visualVocab: Clear labels and structure help people understand.
Emphasis and appeal encourage a decision.
Sequence and signals help people act.
textVocab: Proves ability with a concise action and result.
States a position the text will support.
lab: A notice prioritizes exact usable facts.
At dawn, the empty classroom light switched on.
A story delays explanation to create curiosity.
A call to action makes the desired response clear.
